In September 1880, the St. Louis Choral Society opened as a musical orchestra and choir; the same organization provided annual concerts through 1906, when it was renamed the [St. Louis Symphony Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis_Symphony_Orchestra "St. Louis Symphony Orchestra").[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-mitchell_332-152) Starting in the 1890s, the district known as Chestnut Valley (an area near the present-day [Scottrade Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottrade_Center "Scottrade Center")) became the home of St. Louis ragtime.[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-owsley_gabriels_1-153) Several well-known ragtime and jazz composers lived or played in St. Louis, including [W.C. Handy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W.C._Handy "W.C. Handy"), [Tom Turpin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Turpin "Tom Turpin"), [Scott Hayden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Hayden "Scott Hayden"), [Arthur Marshall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Marshall_(ragtime_composer) "Arthur Marshall (ragtime composer)"), [Joe Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Jordan_(musician) "Joe Jordan (musician)"), and [Louis Chauvin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Chauvin "Louis Chauvin").[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-owsley_gabriels_2-154) In addition to the early Chestnut Valley players, ragtime composer [Scott Joplin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Joplin "Scott Joplin") moved to St. Louis from [Sedalia, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sedalia,_Missouri "Sedalia, Missouri") in 1901, where he associated with Tom Turpin and composed music in the city until moving to Chicago in 1907.[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-owsley_gabriels_6-155)

The sport of [baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baseball "Baseball") began to be played in the years following the Civil War; a team known as the [St. Louis Brown Stockings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis_Brown_Stockings "St. Louis Brown Stockings") was founded in 1875.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-feldmann_8-156) The Brown Stockings were a founding member of the [National League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_League_(baseball) "National League (baseball)") and became a hometown favorite, defeating the Chicago White Stockings (later the [Chicago Cubs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Cubs "Chicago Cubs")) in their opener on May 6, 1875.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_424-157) The original Brown Stockings club closed in 1878, and an unrelated National League team with the same name was founded in 1882.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-feldmann_8-156) This team repeatedly changed its name, shortening to the Browns in 1883, becoming the Perfectos in 1899, and settling on the [St. Louis Cardinals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis_Cardinals "St. Louis Cardinals") in 1900.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-feldmann_8-156) In 1902, a team moved to St. Louis from Milwaukee and adopted the name [St. Louis Browns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis_Browns "St. Louis Browns"), although they had no relation to the previous Browns or Brown Stockings.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-swaine_62-158) From 1902 until the 1950s, St. Louis was home to two Major League teams.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-swaine_62-158)

Notable residents in the field of literature included poets [Sara Teasdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sara_Teasdale "Sara Teasdale") and [T. S. Eliot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._S._Eliot "T. S. Eliot"), as well as playwright [Tennessee Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee_Williams "Tennessee Williams").

### 1904 World's Fair

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_St._Louis&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: 1904 World's Fair")]

Further information: [1904 World's Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1904_World's_Fair "1904 World's Fair")

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ca/Louisiana_Purchase_Exposition_East_Lagoon.jpg/250px-Louisiana_Purchase_Exposition_East_Lagoon.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Louisiana_Purchase_Exposition_East_Lagoon.jpg)

East Lagoon, statue of Saint Louis, Palaces of Education and Manufacture, and wireless telegraph tower.

Beginning in the 1850s, St. Louis hosted annual agricultural and mechanical fairs at [Fairground Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairground_Park "Fairground Park") to connect with regional manufacturers and growers. By the 1880s, the connection to agriculture had declined, and in 1883, a new [St. Louis Exposition and Music Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis_Exposition_and_Music_Hall "St. Louis Exposition and Music Hall") was built to house industrial exhibits.[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_372-159) In 1890, St. Louis attempted to host the [World's Columbian Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_Columbian_Exposition "World's Columbian Exposition"), but the project was awarded to Chicago, which hosted the exposition in 1893.[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_372-159) In 1899, delegates from states that had been part of the Louisiana Purchase met in St. Louis, selecting it as the site of a [world's fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_fair "World's fair") celebrating the centennial of the purchase in 1904.[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_375-160)

Company directors selected the western half of Forest Park as the fair site, sparking a real estate and construction boom.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_376-161) Streetcar and rail service to the area was improved, and a new filtration system was implemented to improve the St. Louis water supply.[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_379-162) The fair consisted of an "Ivory City" of twelve temporary exhibition palaces, and one permanent exhibit palace which became the [St. Louis Art Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis_Art_Museum "St. Louis Art Museum")[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_382-163) after the fair. The fair celebrated American expansionism and world cultures with exhibits of historical French fur-trading, and [Eskimo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eskimo "Eskimo") and [Filipino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filipino_people "Filipino people") villages.[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-arenson_heart_217-164) Concurrently, the [1904 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1904_Summer_Olympics "1904 Summer Olympics") were held in St. Louis, at what would become the campus of [Washington University in St. Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_University_in_St._Louis "Washington University in St. Louis").[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-arenson_heart_218-116)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_St._Louis&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Decline of the inner city and urban renewal: 1905–1980")]

Main article: [History of St. Louis, Missouri (1905–1980)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis,_Missouri_(1905%E2%80%931980) "History of St. Louis, Missouri (1905–1980)")

### Civic improvements and segregation policies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_St._Louis&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Civic improvements and segregation policies")]

During the early 1900s and 1910s, St. Louis began a building program that created parks and playgrounds in several deteriorating residential neighborhoods.[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_397-165) Parks Commissioner (and former [professional tennis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_tennis "History of tennis") player) [Dwight F. Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dwight_F._Davis "Dwight F. Davis") continued the development of recreational facilities during the early 1910s by expanding [tennis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennis "Tennis") facilities and building a public 18-hole [golf course](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golf_course "Golf course") in northwest Forest Park.[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_407-166) The [St. Louis Zoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis_Zoo "St. Louis Zoo") was constructed in Forest Park in the early 1910s under the leadership of Mayor [Henry Kiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Kiel "Henry Kiel").[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_408-167) Since the 1890s, St. Louis had attempted to control its air pollution problems with little success, but damage to buildings and flora made the issue more visible during the 1920s.[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_448-168) Problems came to a head with the [1939 St. Louis smog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1939_St._Louis_smog "1939 St. Louis smog"), which blackened the sky and lasted for three weeks.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_449-169) A ban on burning low-quality coal solved the problem in December 1939, and the addition of [natural gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_gas "Natural gas") for heating assisted homeowners in making the transition to cleaner fuels by the late 1940s.[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_450-170)

[Video 1](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0f/TRooseveltAirplaneRideinStLouis.ogv?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=index&utm_content=original)

President [Theodore Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt "Theodore Roosevelt") became the first president to fly in an airplane while visiting St. Louis in October 1910.

During the 1904 World's Fair, [ballooning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balloon_(aircraft) "Balloon (aircraft)") was demonstrated as a viable means of transportation; in October 1907, the second [Gordon Bennett Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordon_Bennett_Cup_(ballooning) "Gordon Bennett Cup (ballooning)"), an international balloon racing event, was held in the city.[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-mohistflight-171) The first [airplane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airplane "Airplane") flight occurred in late 1909, and by the next year, an [airfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airfield "Airfield") had been established in nearby [Kinloch, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinloch,_Missouri "Kinloch, Missouri").[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-mohistflight-171) In October 1910, St. Louis hosted President [Theodore Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt "Theodore Roosevelt"), who became the first president to fly in an airplane after departing from the field.[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-mohistflight-171)[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-lamberthist-172) In 1925, local [entrepreneur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entrepreneur "Entrepreneur")[Albert Lambert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Bond_Lambert "Albert Bond Lambert") purchased Kinloch Field, expanded its facilities, and renamed it [Lambert Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambert_Field "Lambert Field").[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-mohistflight-171) In May 1927, [Charles Lindbergh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Lindbergh "Charles Lindbergh") departed from Lambert Field en route to New York to begin his solo [non-stop flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-stop_flight "Non-stop flight") across the Atlantic Ocean.[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-lamberthist-172) In early 1928, the city of St. Louis purchased the airport from Lambert, making it the first municipally owned airport in the United States; Lambert remains the area's primary airport.[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-lamberthist-172)

Although St. Louis enforced a variety of [Jim Crow laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Crow_laws "Jim Crow laws"), the area generally had a lower level of racial violence and fewer [lynchings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynchings "Lynchings") than the [American South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_South "American South").[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_410-173) The St. Louis black community was stable and relatively concentrated along the riverfront or near the railroad yards.[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_410-173) Although informal discrimination had existed in the St. Louis housing market since the end of the Civil War, only in 1916 did St. Louis pass a [residential segregation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Residential_segregation "Residential segregation") ordinance.[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_411-174)[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_413-175) The ordinance quickly was invalidated by court [injunctions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Injunctions "Injunctions"), but private [restrictive covenants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Restrictive_covenants "Restrictive covenants") in St. Louis real estate transactions limited the ability of white owners to sell to blacks and were another form of racial discrimination.[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_414-176) In 1948 the U.S. Supreme Court overturned such real estate limitations as unconstitutional in _[Shelley v. Kraemer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelley\_v.\_Kraemer "Shelley v. Kraemer")_, a court case based on the sale of a St. Louis house (the [Shelley House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelley_House_(St._Louis,_Missouri) "Shelley House (St. Louis, Missouri)")) to a black family.

Despite segregationist and racist attitudes, St. Louis acted as a haven during the 1917 [East St. Louis Riot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_St._Louis_Riot "East St. Louis Riot"), as St. Louis police shepherded fleeing blacks across the Eads Bridge to shelter and food provided by the city government and the [American Red Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Red_Cross "American Red Cross").[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_416-177)[Leonidas C. Dyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonidas_C._Dyer "Leonidas C. Dyer"), who represented part of St. Louis in the U.S. House, led a Congressional investigation into the events and eventually sponsored an [anti-lynching bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dyer_Anti-Lynching_Bill "Dyer Anti-Lynching Bill") in response.[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-sullivan_75-178) Due to an influx of refugees from East St. Louis and the general effects of the [Great Migration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Migration_(African_American) "Great Migration (African American)") of blacks from the rural South to industrial cities, the black population of St. Louis increased more rapidly than the whole during the decade of 1910 to 1920.[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_416-177)

The **history of [St. Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis "St. Louis")** began with the settlement of the area by [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas "Indigenous peoples of the Americas")[mound builders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mound_builder_(people) "Mound builder (people)") who lived as part of the [Mississippian culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippian_culture "Mississippian culture") from the 9th century to the 15th century, followed by other migrating tribal groups. Starting in the late 17th century, French explorers arrived. Spain took over in 1763 and a trading company led by [Pierre Laclede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Laclede "Pierre Laclede") and [Auguste Chouteau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auguste_Chouteau "Auguste Chouteau") established the settlement of St. Louis in February 1764. It attracted French settlers leaving Illinois after their [defeat in the Seven Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_in_the_Seven_Years'_War "France in the Seven Years' War"). The city grew in population due to its location as a [trading post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trading_post "Trading post") on the [Mississippi River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River"), as the western fur trade was lucrative. The city played a small role in the [American Revolutionary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War "American Revolutionary War") and became part of the U.S. through the [Louisiana Purchase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_Purchase "Louisiana Purchase") in 1803.

With its connection through the Ohio River to the east, the Mississippi to the south and north, and the Missouri to the west, St. Louis was ideally located to become the main base of interregional trade. In the 1840s, it became a destination for massive immigration by Irish and Germans. Some native-born Americans reacted with fear to the newcomers, adopting [nativist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nativism_(politics) "Nativism (politics)") sentiments. Missouri was a slave state, but the city's proximity to [free states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slave_and_free_states "Slave and free states") caused it to become a center for the filing of [freedom suits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_suits "Freedom suits"). Many slaves gained freedom through such suits in the antebellum years. But, by the 1850s and the [Dred Scott case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dred_Scott_case "Dred Scott case"), interpretations had changed and the [US Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Supreme_Court "US Supreme Court") ruled against him. It also ruled that the Missouri Compromise was unconstitutional, contributing to the tensions causing the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Origins_of_the_American_Civil_War "Origins of the American Civil War"). During the War, St. Louis had a small skirmish on its outskirts, but was held under [Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_(American_Civil_War) "Union (American Civil War)") control.

After the war, the city expanded its railroad connections and industrial activity. It suffered a corresponding rise in [pollution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pollution "Pollution") of the river and waterfront. During the early 1870s, the [Eads Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eads_Bridge "Eads Bridge") was constructed over the Mississippi River, and the city established several large parks, including [Forest Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_Park_(St._Louis) "Forest Park (St. Louis)"). Due to local political and economic disputes, the city separated from [St. Louis County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis_County,_Missouri "St. Louis County, Missouri") in 1876 and became an [independent city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_city_(United_States) "Independent city (United States)"). During the late 19th century, St. Louis became home to two [Major League Baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_League_Baseball "Major League Baseball") teams. [Ragtime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ragtime "Ragtime") and [blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues "Blues") music flourished in the city, with African Americans making major contributions also in [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz").

The city hosted the [1904 World's Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1904_World's_Fair "1904 World's Fair") and the [1904 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1904_Summer_Olympics "1904 Summer Olympics"), attracting millions of visitors. Part of the infrastructure for the fair was the basis for major city institutions in Forest Park. In the early part of the century, many African Americans migrated from the South to the city for industrial jobs, as part of the [Great Migration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Migration_(African_American) "Great Migration (African American)"). St. Louis did not escape the [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression") and its high unemployment. During World War II the city hosted war industries that employed thousands of workers.

After the war, federal highway subsidies and postwar development encouraged outward migration as residents moved to gain newer housing; this [suburbanization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suburbanization "Suburbanization") significantly reduced the city's middle-class population. The city made efforts to create new attractions, such as the [Gateway Arch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gateway_Arch "Gateway Arch"), which construction became a focus of the [civil rights movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_rights_movement "Civil rights movement") to gain desegregated jobs in the skilled trades. The first litigation under the 1964 Civil Rights Act was against St. Louis unions. The city worked to replace substandard housing by new [public housing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_housing "Public housing") projects such as [Pruitt–Igoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pruitt%E2%80%93Igoe "Pruitt–Igoe"). A combination of factors resulted in this being notoriously unsuccessful, and it was demolished in the late 20th century. Starting in the 1980s and continuing into the following century, construction and [gentrification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentrification "Gentrification") have increased in some areas of St. Louis, particularly [downtown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_St._Louis "Downtown St. Louis"). City beautification and crime reduction have made progress, although St. Louis has continued to struggle with crime and perceptions of crime. The city saw modest population growth during the mid-2000s, but showed a decline in the [2010 U.S. census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_U.S._census "2010 U.S. census").

## Exploration and Louisiana before 1762

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_St._Louis&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Exploration and Louisiana before 1762")]

Main article: [History of St. Louis, Missouri before 1762](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis,_Missouri_before_1762 "History of St. Louis, Missouri before 1762")

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/Nouvelle-France_map-en.svg/250px-Nouvelle-France_map-en.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nouvelle-France_map-en.svg)

Map of the British and French settlements in North America in 1750, before the [French and Indian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_and_Indian_War "French and Indian War") (1754 to 1763)

The earliest settlements in the middle [Mississippi Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_Valley "Mississippi Valley") were built in the 10th century by the people of the [Mississippian culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippian_culture "Mississippian culture"), who constructed more than two dozen [platform mounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platform_mounds "Platform mounds") within the area of the future European-American city.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_1-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-peregrine_guide_xx-2) These were related to the center of the culture at the very large complex of [Cahokia Mounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahokia_Mounds "Cahokia Mounds"), on the east side of the Mississippi River. The Mississippian culture ended for unknown reasons in the 14th century and these sites were empty for some time. Native American tribes such as the [Missouria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouria "Missouria") and the [Osage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osage_Nation "Osage Nation") migrated from the eastern Ohio Valley to the [Missouri Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_River_Valley "Missouri River Valley"). They lived in villages along the [Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_River "Missouri River") and [Osage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osage_River "Osage River") rivers.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_1-1) Both groups competed with northeastern tribes such as the [Sauk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sauk_people "Sauk people") and the [Meskwaki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meskwaki "Meskwaki"), and all four groups confronted the earliest European explorers of the middle Mississippi Valley.

Extensive European exploration near the confluence of the Missouri and Mississippi rivers began nearly a century before the city was officially founded.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_2-3) Explorer [Louis Joliet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Joliet "Louis Joliet") and [Jesuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesuit "Jesuit") priest [Jacques Marquette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Marquette "Jacques Marquette") traveled south on the Mississippi River in June 1673, passed the future site of St. Louis and reached the mouth of the [Arkansas River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas_River "Arkansas River") before turning back.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_3-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-shepard_early_10-5)

Nine years later, French explorer [La Salle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9-Robert_Cavelier,_Sieur_de_La_Salle "René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle") led an expedition south from the [Illinois River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois_River "Illinois River") to the mouth of the Mississippi in the [Gulf of Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Mexico "Gulf of Mexico"), claiming the entire valley for France.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_3-4) La Salle named the Mississippi river basin _[La Louisiane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_Louisiane "La Louisiane")_ (Louisiana) after King [Louis XIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XIV "Louis XIV"); the region between and near the confluence of the [Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_River "Ohio River") and Mississippi rivers was named the [Illinois Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois_Country "Illinois Country").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_3-4) As part of a series of forts in the Mississippi valley, the French built settlements at [Cahokia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahokia,_Illinois "Cahokia, Illinois") and [Kaskaskia, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaskaskia,_Illinois "Kaskaskia, Illinois").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_3-4) French trading companies also built towns during the 1720s and 1730s, including [Fort de Chartres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_de_Chartres "Fort de Chartres") and [Ste. Genevieve, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ste._Genevieve,_Missouri "Ste. Genevieve, Missouri"), the first European town in Missouri west of the Mississippi.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_5-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-shepard_early_11-7) From 1756 to 1760, fighting in the [French and Indian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_and_Indian_War "French and Indian War") (the North American front of the [Seven Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Years'_War "Seven Years' War")) halted settlement building. The economy remained weak through 1762 due to the ongoing war, which France lost the following year.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-foley_baron_4-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_8-9)

## City founding and early history: 1763–1803

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_St._Louis&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: City founding and early history: 1763–1803")]

Main article: [History of St. Louis, Missouri (1763–1803)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis,_Missouri_(1763%E2%80%931803) "History of St. Louis, Missouri (1763–1803)")

[![Image 7: Drawing of the St. Louis street grid from the 1780s showing the river and a small village](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/46/Stlouis1780.jpeg/250px-Stlouis1780.jpeg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Stlouis1780.jpeg)

The original St. Louis street grid, ca. 1780

The arrival in New Orleans of [Jean-Jacques Blaise d'Abbadie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Jacques_Blaise_d'Abbadie "Jean-Jacques Blaise d'Abbadie") as the new governor of Louisiana in June 1763 led to changes in colonial policies.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-foley_baron_4-8) D'Abbadie quickly moved to grant trade monopolies in the middle Mississippi Valley to stimulate the economy.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-foley_baron_4-8) Among the new monopolists was [Pierre Laclede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Laclede "Pierre Laclede"), who along with his stepson [Auguste Chouteau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auguste_Chouteau "Auguste Chouteau") set out in August 1763 to build a fur trading post near the confluence of the Missouri and Mississippi rivers.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-foley_baron_4-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_8-9) The settlement of St. Louis was established at a site south of the confluence on the west bank of the Mississippi on February 15, 1764, by Chouteau and a group of about 30 men.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_9-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-foley_baron_5-11) Laclede arrived at the site by mid-1764 and provided detailed plans for the village, including a [street grid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_grid "Street grid") and market area.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-foley_baron_5-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_10-12)

French settlers began to arrive from settlements on the east bank of the Mississippi in 1764, given the transfer of eastern land to [Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Great_Britain "Kingdom of Great Britain") after the [Treaty of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Paris_(1763) "Treaty of Paris (1763)").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_10-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-foley_baron_6-13) The local French lieutenant governor moved to St. Louis in 1765 and began awarding [land grants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_grants "Land grants").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-foley_baron_6-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_15-14) As part of the peace negotiations to end the Seven Years' War, Spain gained control of Louisiana according to the secret [Treaty of Fontainebleau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Fontainebleau_(1762) "Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762)") in 1762.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_17-15) Due to travel times and the [Louisiana Rebellion of 1768](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_Rebellion_of_1768 "Louisiana Rebellion of 1768"), the Spanish took official control in St. Louis only in May 1770.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_22-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-shepard_early_14-17) After the transfer, the Spanish confirmed French land grants, and Spanish soldiers provided local security.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_23-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-shepard_early_15-19)

[![Image 8: Drawing of the first Catholic church in St. Louis showing a small building and a lot](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/First_Catholic_church_in_St_Louis_Missouri.jpg/250px-First_Catholic_church_in_St_Louis_Missouri.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:First_Catholic_church_in_St_Louis_Missouri.jpg)

The first [Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic "Roman Catholic") church in St. Louis, built in 1770

The occupation of most settlers was farming, and by the 1790s nearly 6,000 acres (24 km 2) were under cultivation around St. Louis.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_17-15)[Fur trading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fur_trading "Fur trading") was the major commercial focus of many residents, as it was much more lucrative than agriculture during that period.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_17-15) The residents were not particularly religious, in spite of their [Roman Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic "Roman Catholic") faith.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_31-20) The first church was constructed in mid-1770 and St. Louis acquired a resident priest in 1776, making Catholic religious observance a more customary component of life.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_33-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-shepard_early_19-22)

The French settlers brought both black and Indian [slaves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slaves "Slaves") to St. Louis; although the majority were used as [domestic servants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domestic_servants "Domestic servants"), others worked as agricultural laborers.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-ravens_inf_66-23) In 1769, the Spanish prohibited Indian slavery in Louisiana, but the practice was entrenched among the [French Creoles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_Creole_people "Louisiana Creole people") in St. Louis.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_23-18) As a compromise, Spanish governors ended the Indian slave trade but allowed the retention of current slaves and any children born to them.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_24-24) In 1772, a census determined the population of the village to be 637, including 444 whites (285 males and 159 females) and 193 African slaves, with no Indian slaves reported due to their technical illegality.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_25-25) During the 1770s and 1780s, St. Louis grew slowly and the Spanish commanders were replaced often.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_27-26)

### American Revolutionary War

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_St._Louis&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: American Revolutionary War")]

See also: [Battle of St. Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_St._Louis "Battle of St. Louis")

Upon the beginning of the [American Revolutionary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War "American Revolutionary War"), Spanish governor, Bernardo de Galvez, in New Orleans assisted the [American rebels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_Army "Continental Army") with weapons, food, blankets, tents and ammunition.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_37-27) The Spanish lieutenant governors at St. Louis also aided the Americans, particularly the forces of [George Rogers Clark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Rogers_Clark "George Rogers Clark") during the [Illinois campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois_campaign "Illinois campaign").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_37-27) After the official entry of Spain into the [American Revolutionary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War "American Revolutionary War") in June 1779 on the side of the Americans and the French, the British began preparing an expedition to capture St. Louis and other Mississippi outposts.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-drumm_brits_642-28) However, the city was warned of the plans, and residents began to fortify the town.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-drumm_brits_643-29)

[![Image 9: Painting of the Battle of St. Louis of 1780 showing attacking Native Americans and the defending town](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/St-louis-attack.jpg/250px-St-louis-attack.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:St-louis-attack.jpg)

The [Battle of St. Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_St._Louis "Battle of St. Louis") on May 26, 1780

On May 26, 1780, a British commander leading a force consisting mostly of Indian allies [launched an assault on the town of St. Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_St._Louis "Battle of St. Louis"), but were forced to retreat due to the fortifications constructed by the locals and defections of some of the Indians.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-drumm_brits_644-30) In spite of the failure of their expedition, the Indians managed to torch much of St. Louis' agricultural lands and capture several heads of livestock, alongside several [prisoners of war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prisoners_of_war "Prisoners of war").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-drumm_brits_647-31) A subsequent counterattack launched from the settlers against British forts in the Midwest ended the possibility of another attack being launched on the town.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-drumm_brits_649-32)

After the conclusion of the Revolutionary War at the [Treaty of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Paris_(1783) "Treaty of Paris (1783)"), French Creole families evading American rule moved to the Spanish-controlled land on the west bank, including wealthy merchants [Charles Gratiot, Sr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Gratiot,_Sr. "Charles Gratiot, Sr.") and Gabriel Cerre.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_46-33) Both the Gratiot and Cerre families intermarried with the Chouteau family to create a Creole-dominated society in the 1780s and 1790s. The families also had marital ties to Spanish government officials, including the lieutenant governors Piernas and Cruzat.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_51-34)

### Transfer to France and the United States

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_St._Louis&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Transfer to France and the United States")]

See also: [Three Flags Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Flags_Day "Three Flags Day")

During the 1790s, towns near St. Louis expanded as small farmers sold their lands to the Cerres, Gratiots, Soulards, or Chouteaus. These farmers moved to towns such as [Carondelet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carondelet,_Missouri "Carondelet, Missouri"), [St. Charles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Charles,_Missouri "Saint Charles, Missouri"), and [Florissant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florissant,_Missouri "Florissant, Missouri"). By 1800, only 43% of the district's population lived within the village (1,039 of 2,447).[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_63-35)

The Spanish government secretly returned the unprofitable Louisiana territory to France in October 1800 in the [Treaty of San Ildefonso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Treaty_of_San_Ildefonso "Third Treaty of San Ildefonso").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_68-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-stats_on_unprofit-37) The Spanish officially transferred control in October 1802; however, Spanish administrators remained in charge of St. Louis throughout the time of French ownership.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_68-36) Shortly afterward, a team of American negotiators purchased Louisiana, including St. Louis.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_69-38) On March 8 or 9, 1804, the flag of Spain was lowered at the government buildings in St. Louis and, according to local tradition, the flag of France was raised. On March 10, 1804, the French flag was replaced by that of the United States.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_69-38)

## Expansion, growth, and the Civil War: 1804–1865

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_St._Louis&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Expansion, growth, and the Civil War: 1804–1865")]

Main article: [History of St. Louis, Missouri (1804–1865)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis,_Missouri_(1804%E2%80%931865) "History of St. Louis, Missouri (1804–1865)")

### Government and religion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_St._Louis&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Government and religion")]

Initially, the governor of the [Indiana Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_Territory "Indiana Territory") governed the [Louisiana District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_District "Louisiana District") (which included St. Louis), and the district's organizational law forbade the foreign slave trade and reduced the influence of St. Louis in the region.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_72-39) Wealthy St. Louisans petitioned Congress to review the system, and in July 1805, Congress reorganized the Louisiana District as the [Louisiana Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_Territory "Louisiana Territory"), with its territorial capital at St. Louis and its own territorial governor.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_76-40) From the division of the Louisiana Territory in 1812 to Missouri statehood in 1821, St. Louis was the capital of the [Missouri Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_Territory "Missouri Territory").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-rodriguez_227-41)

[![Image 10: Contemporary photograph of the Old Courthouse in St. Louis showing its dome and expansion wings](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1c/The_Old_Courthouse%2C_Saint_Louis%2C_Missouri.JPG/250px-The_Old_Courthouse%2C_Saint_Louis%2C_Missouri.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Old_Courthouse,_Saint_Louis,_Missouri.JPG)

The [St. Louis Courthouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis_Courthouse "St. Louis Courthouse"), completed in 1828

The population of the city expanded slowly after the Louisiana Purchase, but expansion increased desire to incorporate St. Louis as a town, allowing it to create local ordinances without the approval of the territorial legislature.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_96-42) On November 27, 1809, the first Board of Trustees were elected.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_96-42) The Board passed [slave codes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slave_codes "Slave codes"), created a [volunteer fire department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volunteer_fire_department "Volunteer fire department"), and created an overseer to improve street quality.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_99-43) To enforce town ordinances, the Board created the [St. Louis Police Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis_Police_Department_(Missouri) "St. Louis Police Department (Missouri)"), and a town [jail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jail "Jail") was established in the fortifications built for the Battle of St. Louis.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_97-44)

After the end of the [War of 1812](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_1812 "War of 1812"), the population of St. Louis and the Missouri Territory began expanding quickly.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_104-45) During this expansion land was donated for the [Old St. Louis County Courthouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Courthouse_(St._Louis,_Missouri) "Old Courthouse (St. Louis, Missouri)").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_104-45) The population increase stirred interest in statehood for Missouri, and in 1820, Congress passed the [Missouri Compromise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_Compromise "Missouri Compromise"), authorizing Missouri's admission as a [slave state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slave_state "Slave state").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_116-46) The state constitutional convention and first General Assembly met in St. Louis in 1820.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_117-47) Shortly thereafter, St. Louis incorporated as a city, on December 9, 1822.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_118-119-48) The first mayor of the city was [William Carr Lane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Carr_Lane "William Carr Lane"), and a [Board of Aldermen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_of_Aldermen_of_the_City_of_St._Louis "Board of Aldermen of the City of St. Louis") replaced the earlier Board of Trustees.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_120-49) Early city government focused on improvements to the riverfront and health conditions.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_120-49) In addition to a street paving program, the aldermen voted to rename the streets.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_122-50)

After the transfer of Louisiana to the United States, the Spanish had ended subsidies to the Catholic Church in St. Louis.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_91-51) As a result, Catholics in St. Louis had no resident priest until the arrival of [Louis William Valentine Dubourg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_William_Valentine_Dubourg "Louis William Valentine Dubourg") in early January 1818.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_92-52) Upon his arrival, he replaced the original log chapel with a brick church, recruited priests, and established a seminary.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_93-53) By 1826, a separate [St. Louis diocese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Archdiocese_of_St._Louis "Roman Catholic Archdiocese of St. Louis") was created. [Joseph Rosati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Rosati "Joseph Rosati") became the first bishop in 1827.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_94-54)

[Protestants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestants "Protestants") had received services from itinerant ministers in the late 1790s, but the Spanish required them to move to American territory until after the Louisiana Purchase.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_94-54) After the purchase, the [Baptist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baptist "Baptist") missionary [John Mason Peck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Mason_Peck "John Mason Peck") built the first Protestant church in St. Louis in 1818.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_95-55)[Methodist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodism "Methodism") ministers reached the town during the early years after the purchase, but only formed a congregation in 1821.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_95-55) The [Presbyterian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Church_(U.S.A.) "Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.)") in St. Louis began as a Bible reading society in 1811, and in December 1817 members organized a church and built a chapel late the next year.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_95-55) A fourth Protestant group to take root was the [Episcopal Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_Church_(United_States) "Episcopal Church (United States)"), founded in 1825.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_95-55)

During the 1830s and 1840s, other faith groups also came to St. Louis, including the first [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish "Jewish") congregation in the area, the [United Hebrew Congregation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Hebrew_Congregation_(Chesterfield,_Missouri) "United Hebrew Congregation (Chesterfield, Missouri)"), which was organized in 1837.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-wayman_27-56) Followers of [Mormonism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mormonism "Mormonism") arrived in 1831, and in 1854, they organized the first [LDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Church_of_Jesus_Christ_of_Latter-day_Saints "The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints") church in St. Louis.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-wayman_27-56) Despite these events, during the pre-Civil War era most of the population were culturally Catholic or uninterested in organized religion.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_96-42)

### Commerce, the Panic of 1819, and growth

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_St._Louis&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Commerce, the Panic of 1819, and growth")]

[![Image 11: Drawing of the levee along the Mississippi in 1857 showing steamboats and commercial buildings](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a1/The_Levee_or_Landing%2C_St._Louis%2C_Missouri.jpg/250px-The_Levee_or_Landing%2C_St._Louis%2C_Missouri.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Levee_or_Landing,_St._Louis,_Missouri.jpg)

The St. Louis [levee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levee "Levee") on the Mississippi River in 1857

Commerce after the Louisiana Purchase remained focused on the fur trade; operations in St. Louis were led by the [Chouteau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chouteau "Chouteau") family and its alliance with the Osages and by [Manuel Lisa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Lisa "Manuel Lisa") and his [Missouri Fur Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_Fur_Company "Missouri Fur Company").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_123-57) Due to its role as a major trading post, the city was the departure point for the [Lewis and Clark Expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_and_Clark_Expedition "Lewis and Clark Expedition") in 1804.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-ambrose_133-134-58)

American and other immigrant families began arriving in St. Louis and opening new businesses, including printing and banking, starting in the 1810s. Among the printers was Joseph Charless, who published the first newspaper west of the Mississippi, the _Missouri Gazette_, on July 12, 1808.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_86-59) In 1816 and 1817, groups of merchants formed the first banks in the town, but mismanagement and the [Panic of 1819](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panic_of_1819 "Panic of 1819") led to their closure.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_107-60)

The effect of the Panic of 1819 and subsequent depression slowed commercial activity in St. Louis until the mid-1820s.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_122-50) By 1824 and 1825, however, St. Louis businesses began to recover, largely due to the introduction of the [steamboat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steamboat "Steamboat"); the first to arrive in St. Louis, the _Zebulon M. Pike_, docked on August 2, 1817.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_108-61)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-conard_vol5_139-62)[Rapids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapids "Rapids") north of the city made St. Louis the northernmost [navigable port](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_of_navigation "Head of navigation") for many large riverboats, and the _Pike_ and other ships soon transformed St. Louis into a bustling inland [port](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port "Port").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_135-63)

More goods became available in St. Louis during the economic recovery, largely as a result of the new steamboat power.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_134-64) Wholesalers, new banks, and other retail stores opened starting in the late 1820s and early 1830s.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_141-65) The fur trade continued as a major industry into the 1830s.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_108-61) In 1822, [Jedediah Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jedediah_Smith "Jedediah Smith") joined [William H. Ashley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_H._Ashley "William H. Ashley")'s St. Louis fur trading company.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-66) Smith would later be known for his explorations of the West and for being the first American to travel overland to [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-67) New fur trade companies such as the [Rocky Mountain Fur Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky_Mountain_Fur_Company "Rocky Mountain Fur Company") pioneered trails west.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_126-68) Although [beaver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaver "Beaver") fur lost its popularity in the 1840s, St. Louis continued as a hub of [buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Bison "American Bison")[hide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hide_(skin) "Hide (skin)") and other furs.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_128-69)

Construction of the [County Courthouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Courthouse "County Courthouse") in the late 1820s also encouraged growth, with an addition of western lots to Ninth Street and a new [City Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Hall "City Hall") adjacent to the river in 1833.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_132-70) The military post far north of the city at [Fort Bellefontaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Bellefontaine "Fort Bellefontaine") moved nearer to the city to [Jefferson Barracks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_Barracks "Jefferson Barracks") in 1827, and the [St. Louis Arsenal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis_Arsenal "St. Louis Arsenal") was built in south St. Louis the same year.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-conard_vol2_492-71)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_144-72) The 1830s included dramatic population growth: by 1830, it had increased to 5,832 from roughly 4,500 in 1820. By 1835, it reached 8,316, doubled by 1840 to 16,439, doubled again by 1845 to 35,390, and again by 1850 to 77,860.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_143-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_147-74)

### Infrastructure and education improvements

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_St._Louis&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Infrastructure and education improvements")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/Das_illustrirte_Mississippithal_-_dargestellt_in_80_nach_der_natur_aufgenommenen_ansichten_vom_wasserfalle_zu_St._Anthony_an_bis_zum_gulf_von_Mexico_%281857%29_%2814774698314%29.jpg/250px-thumbnail.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Das_illustrirte_Mississippithal_-_dargestellt_in_80_nach_der_natur_aufgenommenen_ansichten_vom_wasserfalle_zu_St._Anthony_an_bis_zum_gulf_von_Mexico_(1857)_(14774698314).jpg)

[St. Louis Fire (1849)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis_Fire_(1849) "St. Louis Fire (1849)")

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/St._Louis_Levee._1850.jpg/250px-St._Louis_Levee._1850.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:St._Louis_Levee._1850.jpg)

Steamboats along St. Louis Levee, 1850

In large part due to the rapid population growth, [cholera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cholera "Cholera") became a significant problem. In 1849, a major cholera [epidemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epidemic "Epidemic") killed nearly 5,000 people, leading to a new [sewer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sewerage "Sewerage") system and the draining of a mill pond.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_155-75)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_157-76)[Cemeteries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cemetery "Cemetery") were removed to the outskirts to [Bellefontaine Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellefontaine_Cemetery "Bellefontaine Cemetery") and [Calvary Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvary_Cemetery_(St._Louis) "Calvary Cemetery (St. Louis)") to reduce [groundwater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groundwater "Groundwater") contamination.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_146-77) In the same year, a large [fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis_Fire_(1849) "St. Louis Fire (1849)") broke out on a steamboat on the levee, spread to 23 other boats, and destroyed a large portion of the center city.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_167-78) The St. Louis landing was significantly improved during the 1850s. Using the engineering planning of [Robert E. Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Lee "Robert E. Lee"), levees were constructed on the Illinois side to direct water toward Missouri to eliminate sand bars that threatened the landing.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_150-79) Another infrastructure improvement was the city's water system, which was begun in the early 1830s and was continually improved and expanded in the 1840s and 1850s.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_152-80)

Most early St. Louisans remained illiterate through the 1810s, although many wealthy merchants purchased books for private libraries.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_89-81) Early schools in St. Louis were all fee-based and mostly conducted lessons in French.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_90-82) The first substantial educational effort came about under the authority of the Catholic Church, which in 1818 opened Saint Louis Academy, later renamed [Saint Louis University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Louis_University_(United_States) "Saint Louis University (United States)").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_91-51)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-faherty_1968_447-83) In 1832, the college applied for a state [charter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charter "Charter"), and in December 1832, it became the first chartered university west of the Mississippi River.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-faherty_1968_449-84) Its [medical school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_school "Medical school") opened in 1842, with faculty that included [Daniel Brainard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Brainard "Daniel Brainard") (founder of [Rush Medical College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rush_Medical_College "Rush Medical College")), Moses Linton (founder of the first [medical journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_journal "Medical journal") west of the Mississippi River in 1843), and Charles Alexander Pope (later president of the [American Medical Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Medical_Association "American Medical Association")).[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-faherty_1968_450-85) However, the university primarily catered to seminary students rather than the general public, and only in the 1840s did the Catholic Church offer large scale instruction at [parochial schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parochial_schools "Parochial schools").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_91-51)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_166-86) In 1853, [William Greenleaf Eliot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Greenleaf_Eliot "William Greenleaf Eliot") founded a second university in the city – [Washington University in St. Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_University_in_St._Louis "Washington University in St. Louis").[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-ravenswaay_informal_451-87) During the 1850s Eliot founded Smith Academy for boys and Mary Institute for girls, which later merged and became [Mary Institute and St. Louis Country Day School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Institute_and_St._Louis_Country_Day_School "Mary Institute and St. Louis Country Day School").[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-ravenswaay_informal_451-87)

[Public education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_education "Public education") in St. Louis, provided by [St. Louis Public Schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis_Public_Schools "St. Louis Public Schools"), began in 1838 with the creation of two elementary schools, and the system quickly expanded during the 1840s.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_315-88) By 1854, the system had 27 schools and served nearly 4,000 students. In 1855, the district opened a [high school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_school "High school") to considerable fanfare.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_315-88) The high school, now known as [Central VPA High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_VPA_High_School "Central VPA High School"), was the first public high school west of the Mississippi River.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-stlpd11181992-89)[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-stlpd11182004-90) By 1860, nearly 12,000 students had enrolled in the district.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_315-88) The district also opened a [normal school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_school "Normal school") in 1857, which later became [Harris–Stowe State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harris%E2%80%93Stowe_State_University "Harris–Stowe State University").[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_316-91)

Entertainment options increased during the pre–Civil War period; in early 1819, the first theatre production in St. Louis opened, including a musical accompaniment.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-mitchell_331-92) In the late 1830s, a 35-member [orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchestra "Orchestra") briefly played in St. Louis, and in 1860, another orchestra opened that played more than 60 concerts through 1870.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-mitchell_331-92)

### Slavery, immigration and nativism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_St._Louis&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Slavery, immigration and nativism")]

See also: [History of slavery in Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_slavery_in_Missouri "History of slavery in Missouri")

[![Image 14: Painting of Dred Scott](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/Oil_on_Canvas_Portrait_of_Dred_Scott_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Oil_on_Canvas_Portrait_of_Dred_Scott_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Oil_on_Canvas_Portrait_of_Dred_Scott_(cropped).jpg)

[Dred Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dred_Scott "Dred Scott"), whose famous [case to gain his freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dred_Scott_v._Sandford "Dred Scott v. Sandford") began as a lawsuit filed in St. Louis in 1846

Missouri was admitted as a [slave state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_and_slave_states "Free and slave states"). During the 1840s, the number of slaves increased but their percentage relative to the population declined; during the 1850s, both the number and percentage declined.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_179-93) Roughly 3,200 free blacks and slaves lived in St. Louis in 1850, working as domestic servants, artisans, crew on the riverboats and [stevedores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stevedores "Stevedores").[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_179-93)

Some slaves were allowed to earn wages, and some were able to save money to purchase their freedom or that of relatives.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-hodes_rising_20-94) Others were [manumitted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manumission "Manumission"), which occurred relatively more frequently in St. Louis than in the surrounding rural areas.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_179-93) Still others attempted to escape via the [Underground Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underground_Railroad "Underground Railroad") or attempted to gain their freedom through [freedom suits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_suits "Freedom suits").[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-hodes_rising_18-95) The first freedom suit in St. Louis was filed by [Marguerite Scypion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marguerite_Scypion "Marguerite Scypion") in 1805. More than 300 suits were filed in St. Louis before the Civil War.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-park_service-96) Among the most famous was that of [Dred Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dred_Scott "Dred Scott") and his wife Harriet, in [a case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dred_Scott_v._Sandford "Dred Scott v. Sandford") heard at the Old Courthouse. The suit was based on their having traveled and lived with their master in free states. Although the state ruled in his favor, an appeal to the [U.S. Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Supreme_Court "U.S. Supreme Court") resulted in an 1857 ruling against them. The Court ruled that slaves could not be counted as citizens, overturning the basis of the [Missouri Compromise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_Compromise "Missouri Compromise") and inflaming national debate about slavery.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-97)

During the economic expansion of the 1830s, Irish and German immigration to St. Louis increased substantially.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-hodes_rising_8-98) In particular, the writings of [Gottfried Duden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gottfried_Duden "Gottfried Duden") encouraged German immigration.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-hodes_rising_11-99) Many Irish were motivated by the [Great Famine of 1845–1846](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Famine_(Ireland) "Great Famine (Ireland)") and the failed [Irish uprising of 1848](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young_Irelander_Rebellion_of_1848 "Young Irelander Rebellion of 1848").[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_164-100)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-faherty_irish_xi-101) Other Irish settlers came because of its reputation as a Catholic city.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-faherty_irish_12-102)

[Nativist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nativism_(politics) "Nativism (politics)") sentiment increased in St. Louis during the late 1840s, leading to mob attacks and [riots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riot "Riot") in 1844, 1849, and 1852.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_165-103) The 1844 riots derived from popular outrage and resentment toward human [dissection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissection "Dissection"), which was then taking place at the Saint Louis University Medical College.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-conard_vol_4_1913-104) The discovery of human remains prompted rumors of [grave robbing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grave_robbing "Grave robbing"), and a mob of more than 3,000 residents attacked the medical college, destroying most of its interior facilities.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-conard_vol_4_1914-105) The worst nativist riot in St. Louis took place in 1854. The local [militia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Militia "Militia") was used to end the fighting.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_171-106) 10 people were killed, 33 wounded, and 93 buildings were damaged. Regulations on elections prevented fighting in future elections in 1856 and 1858.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_172-107)

### American Civil War

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_St._Louis&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: American Civil War")]

Further information: [St. Louis in the Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis_in_the_Civil_War "St. Louis in the Civil War")

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/Painting_%22The_Last_Sale_of_Slaves%22_by_Thomas_Satterwhite_Noble.jpg/250px-Painting_%22The_Last_Sale_of_Slaves%22_by_Thomas_Satterwhite_Noble.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Painting_%22The_Last_Sale_of_Slaves%22_by_Thomas_Satterwhite_Noble.jpg)

[Slave auction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slave_markets_and_slave_jails_in_the_United_States "Slave markets and slave jails in the United States") in 1861 in Saint-Louis, by [Thomas Satterwhite Noble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Satterwhite_Noble "Thomas Satterwhite Noble")

Before the war, the core of St. Louis leadership had shifted from the Creole and Irish families to a new group, dominated by anti-slavery Germans.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_229-108) Among this new class of leaders was [Frank P. Blair Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_P._Blair_Jr.?action=edit&redlink=1 "Frank P. Blair Jr. (page does not exist)"), who led an effort to create a local militia loyal to the Union after Missouri Governor [Claiborne Fox Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claiborne_Fox_Jackson "Claiborne Fox Jackson") hinted about [secession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secession "Secession").[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_232-109) This local militia allied itself with the Union army forces at Jefferson Barracks under the leadership of [Nathaniel Lyon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathaniel_Lyon "Nathaniel Lyon"), which on May 10, 1861, cleared a [Confederate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederate_States_of_America "Confederate States of America") encampment outside the city in what became known as the [Camp Jackson Affair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camp_Jackson_Affair "Camp Jackson Affair").[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_236-110) While the Confederates were being marched back into town, a group of citizens attacked the Union and militia forces, costing 28 civilian lives.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_237-111)

Throughout the entirety of the Civil War, and despite having seen no battles, St. Louis was under pressure as it was considered a city on the borderline. Though many people were confident in abolition, many were concerned about the economic effect of losing their free work force. In addition, St. Louis was still a developing city, and so a war could lead to utter destruction and ruin. However, with all the necessity of ammunition, St. Louis survived and transformed into a leader among cities.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-112)

After the Camp Jackson Affair, there were no more military threats to Union control until 1864, although [guerrilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guerrilla "Guerrilla") activity continued in rural areas for the duration of the war.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_237-111) Union General [John C. Frémont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_C._Fr%C3%A9mont "John C. Frémont") placed the city under [martial law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martial_law "Martial law") in August 1861 to suppress [sedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sedition "Sedition"); after Fremont's dismissal, Union army forces continued to suppress pro-Confederate demonstrations.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_242-113) The war significantly damaged St. Louis commerce, especially after the Confederacy blockaded the Mississippi shutting off St. Louis's connection to eastern markets.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_255-114) War also slowed growth during the 1860s, with an increase of only 43,000 residents from 1860 to 1866.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_265-115)

## Fourth city status: 1866–1904

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_St._Louis&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Fourth city status: 1866–1904")]

Main article: [History of St. Louis, Missouri (1866–1904)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis,_Missouri_(1866%E2%80%931904) "History of St. Louis, Missouri (1866–1904)")

During the decades after the Civil War, St. Louis grew to become the nation's fourth largest city, after New York City, Philadelphia, and Chicago.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-arenson_heart_218-116) It also experienced rapid infrastructure and transportation development and the growth of heavy industry. The period culminated with the [1904 World's Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_Purchase_Exposition "Louisiana Purchase Exposition") and [1904 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1904_Summer_Olympics "1904 Summer Olympics"), which were held concurrently in St. Louis.

### Infrastructure, parks, and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_St._Louis&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Infrastructure, parks, and education")]

[![Image 16: Photograph of the Eads Bridge under construction in 1874 showing its girders and piers](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/Eads_Bridge_construction.jpg/250px-Eads_Bridge_construction.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Eads_Bridge_construction.jpg)

The [Eads Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eads_Bridge "Eads Bridge") opened in 1874 as the first St. Louis bridge over the [Mississippi River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River").

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/39/4th_Fa._Chesnut_N._1872.jpg/250px-4th_Fa._Chesnut_N._1872.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:4th_Fa._Chesnut_N._1872.jpg)

4th Fa. Chesnut N., 1872

During the Civil War, the infrastructure of St. Louis suffered from neglect; another cholera epidemic struck in 1866, and [typhoid fever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typhoid_fever "Typhoid fever") raged.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_266-117) In response, St. Louis improved its water system and established a Board of Health to regulate polluting industries.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-hurley_nui_152-118)[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_267-119) St. Louis's park system was expanded during the 1860s and 1870s, with the creation of [Tower Grove Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_Grove_Park "Tower Grove Park") and [Forest Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_Park_(St._Louis,_Missouri) "Forest Park (St. Louis, Missouri)").[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_St._Louis#cite_note-primm_lion_306-120)

### Railroads

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_St._Louis&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Railroads")]
