| National average | 8.7% | 15.9% | 24.9% |
| St. Louis (total) | 9.8% | 24% | 35% |
| St. Louis (blacks) | 13.2% | 42.8% | 80% |

When World War I started in 1914, both the German and Irish communities in St. Louis wanted the U.S. to stay [neutral](https://kids.kiddle.co/Neutrality_(international_relations) "Neutrality (international relations)"). This led to more nativism after the U.S. entered the war in 1917. German St. Louisans faced some discrimination, and German culture was suppressed. Business was not greatly affected by the war. However, the population started to decrease as men were needed for factories closer to the Atlantic.

In response to the [1918 influenza pandemic](https://kids.kiddle.co/Spanish_flu "Spanish flu"), the Health Commissioner, Dr. Max C. Starkloff, closed all public places in October 1918. He also banned public gatherings of more than 20 people. His actions are seen as an early example of [social distancing](https://kids.kiddle.co/Social_distancing "Social distancing"). St. Louis had half the death rate compared to other cities that did not take such measures.

After World War I, the nationwide [prohibition of alcohol](https://kids.kiddle.co/Prohibition_Era "Prohibition Era") in 1919 caused big losses for the St. Louis brewing industry. Other industries, like clothing manufacturing, car making, and chemical production, filled much of the gap. St. Louis's economy was quite diverse and healthy in the 1920s.

St. Louis suffered as much as or more than other cities during the early years of the [Great Depression](https://kids.kiddle.co/Great_Depression "Great Depression"). Factory output fell by 57 percent between 1929 and 1933. Unemployment was high in most cities, and St. Louis was no different (see table). Black workers in St. Louis faced much higher unemployment than white workers. To help the unemployed, the city started giving money for [relief operations](https://kids.kiddle.co/Humanitarian_aid "Humanitarian aid") in 1930. [New Deal](https://kids.kiddle.co/New_Deal "New Deal") programs, like the [Public Works Administration](https://kids.kiddle.co/Public_Works_Administration "Public Works Administration"), also employed thousands of St. Louisans. Construction jobs helped reduce the number of people needing direct relief by the late 1930s.

### World War II and Its Aftermath

[![Image 15: Butch OHare F6F-3](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/1/15/Butch_OHare_F6F-3.jpg/300px-Butch_OHare_F6F-3.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Butch_OHare_F6F-3.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Butch_OHare_F6F-3.jpg "Enlarge")

[Edward "Butch" O'Hare](https://kids.kiddle.co/Edward_O%27Hare "Edward O'Hare") was a well-known St. Louis [flying ace](https://kids.kiddle.co/Flying_ace "Flying ace") in World War II.

During World War II, St. Louis had a large ammunition factory and the Curtiss-Wright aircraft factory. Area factories also made uniforms, shoes, [K-rations](https://kids.kiddle.co/K-ration "K-ration"), chemicals, and medicines. The [uranium](https://kids.kiddle.co/Uranium "Uranium") used in the [Manhattan Project](https://kids.kiddle.co/Manhattan_Project "Manhattan Project") was processed in St. Louis by Mallinckrodt Chemical Company starting in 1942. Several [atomic bomb](https://kids.kiddle.co/Nuclear_weapon "Nuclear weapon") scientists had ties to St. Louis. At the start of the war, many German, Italian, and Japanese St. Louisans were questioned or arrested. The [FBI](https://kids.kiddle.co/Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation "Federal Bureau of Investigation") investigated claims of disloyalty in the area. Residents practiced [civil defense](https://kids.kiddle.co/Civil_defense "Civil defense") drills and supported the war effort by collecting scrap and buying war bonds. St. Louis produced several notable soldiers, including [Edward O'Hare](https://kids.kiddle.co/Edward_O%27Hare "Edward O'Hare"), who won the [Medal of Honor](https://kids.kiddle.co/Medal_of_Honor "Medal of Honor"). [Wendell O. Pruitt](https://kids.kiddle.co/Wendell_O._Pruitt "Wendell O. Pruitt"), an [African-American](https://kids.kiddle.co/African_Americans "African Americans") pilot, also achieved great success.

At the start of the war, African-American workers gained more acceptance in industry. But discrimination was still a problem. During the war, city officials passed the first city integration law. It allowed African Americans to eat at city-owned lunch counters, but not private ones. In May 1944, a Black sailor in uniform was refused service at a private lunch counter. This led to peaceful [sit-in](https://kids.kiddle.co/Sit-in "Sit-in") protests at downtown diners. No changes to Jim Crow segregation at lunch counters happened immediately. However, Saint Louis University admitted its first Black students in August 1944.

More than 5,400 St. Louisans were killed or went missing in the war. The end of the war led to many St. Louis factories closing. Major [layoffs](https://kids.kiddle.co/Layoff "Layoff") began in May and continued through August 1945. By late 1945, returning soldiers faced a shortage of housing and jobs. The GI Bill allowed many St. Louis veterans to buy homes and go to college. This encouraged people to move to the suburbs, which reduced the city's population after the war.

### Moving to the Suburbs and Population Loss

People moving westward from St. Louis had been happening since the city's early days. But it sped up in the late 1800s. Starting in the 1890s, the [St. Louis streetcar system](https://kids.kiddle.co/Streetcars_in_St._Louis "Streetcars in St. Louis") and commuter train stations allowed people to travel from suburban towns into downtown. Towns like [Kirkwood](https://kids.kiddle.co/Kirkwood,_Missouri "Kirkwood, Missouri"), [Maplewood](https://kids.kiddle.co/Maplewood,_Missouri "Maplewood, Missouri"), and [Webster Groves](https://kids.kiddle.co/Webster_Groves,_Missouri "Webster Groves, Missouri") grew quickly between 1900 and 1930. This movement to these towns doubled the population of St. Louis County from 1910 to 1920. Meanwhile, the city only grew by 12 percent.

In the 1930s, the city's population decreased slightly for the first time. But St. Louis County grew by nearly 30 percent. Almost 80 percent of new homes in the region were built outside city limits in the late 1930s. St. Louis city planners could not stop this by adding more land to the city.

The city reached its highest population in 1950, with 856,796 residents. It peaked in the early 1950s with about 880,000 people. However, new highways and more car ownership allowed even more people to move to the suburbs. The city's population began a long decline. Another reason for the population loss was [white flight](https://kids.kiddle.co/White_flight "White flight"). This began in the late 1950s and continued through the 1960s and 1970s. From 1950 to 1960, the city population dropped by 13 percent. From 1960 to 1970, it dropped another 17 percent. Most of this decline was white residents moving out, mainly to the suburbs.

Between 1960 and 1970, 34 percent of white city residents moved out. Also, more white people died than were born in the city. By the early 1970s, the white population had decreased significantly, especially among young adults. The Black population of St. Louis grew by 19.5 percent in the 1960s. During that decade, the percentage of Black city residents rose from 29 to 41 percent. However, the Black population also decreased from 1968 to 1972, with many Black residents moving out of the city to suburban areas in St. Louis County.

### City Renewal Projects and the Gateway Arch

[![Image 16: St. Louis riverfront after demolition for Gateway Arch (1942)](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/6/62/St._Louis_riverfront_after_demolition_for_Gateway_Arch_%281942%29.jpg/300px-St._Louis_riverfront_after_demolition_for_Gateway_Arch_%281942%29.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:St._Louis_riverfront_after_demolition_for_Gateway_Arch_(1942).jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:St._Louis_riverfront_after_demolition_for_Gateway_Arch_(1942).jpg "Enlarge")

 The St. Louis riverfront in 1942 after land was cleared for [Gateway Arch National Park](https://kids.kiddle.co/Gateway_Arch_National_Park "Gateway Arch National Park")

Early efforts to improve St. Louis happened at the same time as plans to build a [riverfront memorial](https://kids.kiddle.co/Gateway_Arch_National_Park "Gateway Arch National Park") to honor Thomas Jefferson. This memorial would later include the famous [Gateway Arch](https://kids.kiddle.co/Gateway_Arch "Gateway Arch"). Work began in the early 1930s to buy and tear down buildings in a forty-block area where the memorial would stand. The only part of the original street grid that remained was north of the Eads Bridge. The only building left in the area was the [Old Cathedral](https://kids.kiddle.co/Basilica_of_St._Louis,_King_of_France "Basilica of St. Louis, King of France"). Demolition continued until World War II. After the war, the area was used as a parking lot.

The project stalled until a design competition for the memorial was held. In 1948, Finnish architect [Eero Saarinen](https://kids.kiddle.co/Eero_Saarinen "Eero Saarinen")'s design for a tall, curved arch won. However, construction didn't start until 1954. The Arch was completed in October 1965. A museum and visitors' center opened underneath it in 1976. The Arch attracted millions of visitors. It also led to over $500 million in downtown construction in the 1970s and 1980s.

Along with plans for the Gateway Arch, there were plans to build [subsidized housing](https://kids.kiddle.co/Subsidized_housing "Subsidized housing") in the city in the 1930s. Despite city improvements in the 1920s and two housing projects built in 1939, many houses after World War II still lacked basic facilities. Thousands of St. Louisans lived in crowded, unsafe conditions.

Starting in 1953, St. Louis cleared the Chestnut Valley area in Midtown. The land was sold to developers who built middle-class apartment buildings. Nearby, the city cleared over 450 acres (1.8 km2) of a neighborhood called Mill Creek Valley. This displaced thousands of people. A mixed-income housing development called LaClede Town was built there in the early 1960s. However, this was later torn down for a Saint Louis University expansion. Most people displaced from Mill Creek Valley were poor and African American. They often moved to stable, middle-class Black neighborhoods like The Ville.

[![Image 17: Pruitt-Igoe 1968March03](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/0/09/Pruitt-Igoe_1968March03.jpg/300px-Pruitt-Igoe_1968March03.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Pruitt-Igoe_1968March03.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Pruitt-Igoe_1968March03.jpg "Enlarge")

 The [Pruitt–Igoe](https://kids.kiddle.co/Pruitt%E2%80%93Igoe "Pruitt–Igoe")[housing project](https://kids.kiddle.co/Public_housing "Public housing") (shown from above) consisted of 33 buildings and nearly 3,000 units but lasted less than 20 years

In 1953, St. Louis issued bonds to fund the [St. Louis Gateway Mall](https://kids.kiddle.co/St._Louis_Gateway_Mall "St. Louis Gateway Mall") project and several new high-rise housing projects. The most famous and largest was [Pruitt–Igoe](https://kids.kiddle.co/Pruitt%E2%80%93Igoe "Pruitt–Igoe"). It opened in 1954 on the northwest edge of downtown. It had 33 eleven-story buildings with nearly 3,000 units. Between 1953 and 1957, St. Louis built over 6,100 public housing units. They opened with excitement from leaders, the media, and new residents.

But problems quickly appeared. There was too little recreational space, not enough healthcare or shopping centers, and few job opportunities. Crime was widespread, especially at Pruitt–Igoe. That complex was torn down in 1975. Other St. Louis housing projects remained mostly full through the 1980s, despite ongoing crime problems.

Along with housing projects, a 1955 urban renewal bond issue provided over $110 million. These funds bought land to build three expressways into downtown St. Louis. These later became [Interstate 64](https://kids.kiddle.co/Interstate_64 "Interstate 64"), [Interstate 70](https://kids.kiddle.co/Interstate_70 "Interstate 70"), and [Interstate 44](https://kids.kiddle.co/Interstate_44 "Interstate 44"). In 1967, the Poplar Street Bridge opened. It carried traffic from all three expressways over the Mississippi River. The Arch opened in 1965, and the bridge in 1967. A new [stadium](https://kids.kiddle.co/Stadium "Stadium") for the St. Louis Cardinals also opened. The Cardinals moved into Busch Memorial Stadium in 1966. Building the stadium required tearing down Chinatown, St. Louis, ending the Chinese immigrant community that had been there for decades.

## Recent Times: 1981–Present

### School Desegregation and Transfers

Even though official segregation in St. Louis public schools ended in 1954, after _[Brown v. Board of Education](https://kids.kiddle.co/Brown\_v.\_Board\_of\_Education "Brown v. Board of Education")_, some St. Louis area educators still used tactics to keep schools separated by race in the 1960s.

In the 1970s, a [lawsuit](https://kids.kiddle.co/Lawsuit "Lawsuit") challenged this segregation. This led to a 1983 agreement. St. Louis County school districts agreed to accept Black students from the city on a voluntary basis. State money was used to transport students to provide an integrated education. The agreement also asked white students from the county to voluntarily attend city magnet schools. This was an effort to desegregate the city's remaining schools.

Despite opposition from state and local leaders, the plan greatly desegregated St. Louis schools. In 1980, 82 percent of Black students in the city attended all-Black schools. By 1995, only 41 percent did. In the late 1990s, the St. Louis voluntary transfer program was the largest of its kind in the United States. Over 14,000 students were enrolled.

A new agreement in 1999 allowed most St. Louis County districts to continue participating. However, they could reduce the number of incoming transfer students starting in 2002. Districts have been allowed to reduce available seats in the program by five percent each year since 1999. A five-year extension was approved in 2007, and another in 2012. This allowed new students to enroll through the 2018–2019 school year.

Critics say that most of the desegregation happens when Black students transfer to the county, not when white students transfer to the city. Another criticism is that the program weakens city schools by taking away talented students. Despite these issues, the program will continue until all transfer students graduate. With the last group of transfer students allowed to enroll in 2018–2019, the program will end after the 2030–2031 school year.

### New Buildings and City Improvements

From 1981 to 1993, new construction projects started downtown. This was the most activity since the early 1960s. One of these was the city's tallest building, [One Metropolitan Square](https://kids.kiddle.co/One_Metropolitan_Square "One Metropolitan Square"), built in 1989. New shopping areas also began to appear. [Amtrak](https://kids.kiddle.co/Amtrak "Amtrak") stopped using Union Station as a passenger train terminal in 1978. But in 1985, it reopened as a festival marketplace. The same year, developers opened [St. Louis Centre](https://kids.kiddle.co/One_City_Center_(St._Louis) "One City Center (St. Louis)"), a large four-story [shopping mall](https://kids.kiddle.co/Mall "Mall").

By the late 1990s, however, the mall became less popular. This was due to the expansion of the [St. Louis Galleria](https://kids.kiddle.co/Saint_Louis_Galleria "Saint Louis Galleria") in [Brentwood, Missouri](https://kids.kiddle.co/Brentwood,_Missouri "Brentwood, Missouri"). The mall's main store closed in 2001. The mall itself closed in 2006. Starting in 2010, developers began turning the mall into a parking garage. An adjoining building was converted into apartments, a hotel, and shops.

[![Image 18: St. Louis MO Ralph Moran](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/5/55/St._Louis_MO_Ralph_Moran.jpg/300px-St._Louis_MO_Ralph_Moran.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:St._Louis_MO_Ralph_Moran.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:St._Louis_MO_Ralph_Moran.jpg "Enlarge")

 The [Washington Avenue Historic District](https://kids.kiddle.co/Washington_Avenue_Historic_District_(St._Louis,_Missouri) "Washington Avenue Historic District (St. Louis, Missouri)") has seen many renovation projects since the late 1990s.

The city also supported a major expansion of the St. Louis Convention Center in the 1980s. City leaders focused on keeping professional sports teams. To do this, the city bought [The Arena](https://kids.kiddle.co/St._Louis_Arena "St. Louis Arena"). This was a 15,000-seat venue for professional [ice hockey](https://kids.kiddle.co/Ice_hockey "Ice hockey"), home to the [St. Louis Blues](https://kids.kiddle.co/St._Louis_Blues "St. Louis Blues"). In the early 1990s, leaders worked with businesses to build a new [ice hockey](https://kids.kiddle.co/Ice_hockey "Ice hockey") arena. This arena, now called the [Enterprise Center](https://kids.kiddle.co/Enterprise_Center "Enterprise Center"), was built on the site of the city's Kiel Auditorium. The developers promised to renovate the nearby [opera house](https://kids.kiddle.co/Opera_house "Opera house").

The arena opened in 1994. The original arena was torn down in 1999. But renovations on the opera house didn't start until 2007, more than 15 years later. The [Peabody Opera House](https://kids.kiddle.co/Stifel_Theatre "Stifel Theatre") reopened on October 1, 2011.

In January 1995, the owner of the [National Football League](https://kids.kiddle.co/National_Football_League "National Football League") team, the Los Angeles Rams, announced they would move to St. Louis. The team replaced the St. Louis Cardinals, an NFL team that had moved to Arizona in 1988. The Rams played their first game in their St. Louis stadium, [The Dome at America's Center](https://kids.kiddle.co/The_Dome_at_America%27s_Center "The Dome at America's Center"), on October 22, 1996.

Starting in the early 1980s, more renovation and construction projects began. Some are still unfinished. In 1981, the [Fox Theatre](https://kids.kiddle.co/Fox_Theatre_(St._Louis) "Fox Theatre (St. Louis)"), a movie theater that closed in 1978, was fully restored. It reopened as a [performing arts](https://kids.kiddle.co/Performing_arts "Performing arts") venue.

One area that saw major changes was the [Washington Avenue Historic District](https://kids.kiddle.co/Washington_Avenue_Historic_District_(St._Louis,_Missouri) "Washington Avenue Historic District (St. Louis, Missouri)"). This area runs along Washington Avenue for almost two dozen blocks. In the early 1990s, clothing manufacturers moved out of the large office buildings there. By the end of that decade, developers began turning the buildings into lofts (apartments). Prices for these spaces increased greatly. By 2001, nearly 280 apartments were built. One project still being developed is the Mercantile Exchange Building. It is being converted into offices, apartments, shops, and a movie theater. These changes have also increased the downtown population. Both the central business district and Washington Avenue district more than doubled their populations from 2000 to 2010.

Other downtown projects include the renovation of the [Old Post Office](https://kids.kiddle.co/United_States_Customhouse_and_Post_Office_(St._Louis,_Missouri) "United States Customhouse and Post Office (St. Louis, Missouri)"). This started in 1998 and finished in 2006. The Old Post Office and seven nearby buildings had been empty since the early 1990s. By 2010, this complex had various tenants. These included a branch of the [St. Louis Public Library](https://kids.kiddle.co/St._Louis_Public_Library "St. Louis Public Library"), a branch of Webster University, and government offices. The Old Post Office renovation led to the development of a nearby plaza. This plaza is connected to a new $80 million residential building called Roberts Tower. It was the first new residential building in downtown St. Louis since the 1970s.

As early as 1999, the St. Louis Cardinals started pushing for a new [Busch Stadium](https://kids.kiddle.co/Busch_Stadium "Busch Stadium"). This was part of a trend in [Major League Baseball](https://kids.kiddle.co/Major_League_Baseball "Major League Baseball") to build new stadiums. In early 2002, plans for a new park were agreed upon by state and local leaders and the Cardinals owners. The Cardinals agreed to build a mixed-use development called St. Louis Ballpark Village. This would be on part of the old Busch Memorial Stadium site. The new stadium opened in 2006. Construction for Ballpark Village began in February 2013.

St. Louis is known for its [architecture](https://kids.kiddle.co/Architecture_of_St._Louis "Architecture of St. Louis"). In recent years, there has been a growing movement for historic preservation. An organization called the National Building Arts Center supports this effort.

# History of St. Louis facts for kids

[Kids Encyclopedia Facts](https://kids.kiddle.co/)

The **history of [St. Louis](https://kids.kiddle.co/St._Louis "St. Louis")** is a long and exciting story! It began with ancient Native American people who built large mounds here. Later, French explorers arrived, and then Spain took control. In 1764, a trading company founded the city of St. Louis. Many French settlers moved here after France lost a big war.

St. Louis grew quickly because it was a great [trading post](https://kids.kiddle.co/Trading_post "Trading post") on the [Mississippi River](https://kids.kiddle.co/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River"). The fur trade was very profitable. The city became part of the U.S. after the [Louisiana Purchase](https://kids.kiddle.co/Louisiana_Purchase "Louisiana Purchase") in 1803. Its location made it a major center for trade between different regions.

In the 1840s, many Irish and German immigrants came to St. Louis. Missouri was a state where slavery was allowed, but St. Louis was close to states where slavery was illegal. This led to many enslaved people trying to gain their freedom through lawsuits. One famous case was [Dred Scott](https://kids.kiddle.co/Dred_Scott "Dred Scott")'s, which went all the way to the [US Supreme Court](https://kids.kiddle.co/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States"). The court's decision made tensions about slavery even worse, leading to the [American Civil War](https://kids.kiddle.co/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"). St. Louis stayed under [Union](https://kids.kiddle.co/Union_(American_Civil_War) "Union (American Civil War)") control during the war.

After the war, St. Louis built more railroads and factories. The [Eads Bridge](https://kids.kiddle.co/Eads_Bridge "Eads Bridge") was built over the Mississippi River in the 1870s. The city also created large parks like [Forest Park](https://kids.kiddle.co/Forest_Park_(St._Louis) "Forest Park (St. Louis)"). In 1876, St. Louis separated from [St. Louis County](https://kids.kiddle.co/St._Louis_County,_Missouri "St. Louis County, Missouri") to become its own independent city. This limited its growth later on. By the late 1800s, St. Louis was home to two [Major League Baseball](https://kids.kiddle.co/Major_League_Baseball "Major League Baseball") teams. [Ragtime](https://kids.kiddle.co/Ragtime "Ragtime") and [blues](https://kids.kiddle.co/Blues "Blues") music became popular here, with African Americans playing a huge role.

St. Louis hosted the [1904 World's Fair](https://kids.kiddle.co/Louisiana_Purchase_Exposition "Louisiana Purchase Exposition") and the [1904 Summer Olympics](https://kids.kiddle.co/1904_Summer_Olympics "1904 Summer Olympics"), bringing millions of visitors. Many African Americans moved to the city for factory jobs during the [Great Migration](https://kids.kiddle.co/Great_Migration_(African_American) "Great Migration (African American)"). The city faced tough times during the [Great Depression](https://kids.kiddle.co/Great_Depression "Great Depression") and then helped with war industries during World War II.

After the war, many people moved to the suburbs. The city built new attractions like the [Gateway Arch](https://kids.kiddle.co/Gateway_Arch "Gateway Arch"). Its construction became important for the [civil rights movement](https://kids.kiddle.co/Civil_Rights_Movement "Civil Rights Movement") as people fought for fair jobs. The city also tried to build new [public housing](https://kids.kiddle.co/Public_housing "Public housing") projects, but some, like [Pruitt–Igoe](https://kids.kiddle.co/Pruitt%E2%80%93Igoe "Pruitt–Igoe"), didn't work out well and were torn down. Since the 1980s, parts of St. Louis, especially [downtown](https://kids.kiddle.co/Downtown_St._Louis "Downtown St. Louis"), have seen new construction and improvements. The city is still working to reduce crime and make the city even better.
